anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine runtime settings (memory, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, creating artificial pressure or idle gaps that do not reflect real resource limits.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions block or spin while fighting for access to hot buffer-cache pages, page pins, or latches, causing serialization inside the buffer manager rather than at the row-lock layer.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical devices or virtual storage layers hit their bandwidth / IOPS ceiling, stretching read- and write-latencies and driving up I/O wait times.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits a confused mix of symptoms:  • Bursts of buffer-busy, page-latch, log-write, and file-I/O waits appear side-by-side.  • Checkpoint or background-writer storms trigger prolonged dirty-page flushing that holds buffer latches, freezes modifying sessions, and inflates read/write latency at the device.  • CPU alternates between under-utilization (blocked on I/O) and futile spin-loops (contending for latches), while overall throughput collapses and response-time variance widens.  • Wait-event histograms show both high in-engine spin / latch time and deep storage queue depths, yet OS-level memory and CPU headroom remain.

Causal chain: Misaligned configuration parameters—such as too small a buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint intervals, or an undersized async I/O batch size—force pages to be evicted and flushed more often than necessary. The heightened flush frequency drives up physical I/O, quickly exhausting the storage subsystem’s throughput budget and inflating device latency. Slower I/O prolongs dirty-page residency and latch hold times, intensifying buffer and latch contention. In turn, the elevated contention magnifies the sensitivity to the original configuration errors, prompting more retries, spin-loops, and timeout-driven flushes. The feedback loop between bad configuration, I/O saturation, and internal latch contention compounds stalls across all sessions, degrading both transactional and analytical workloads simultaneously.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
